screens.title: Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer
screens.narratorSegment: Multiplayer architecture defines who holds the truth about the game world. In a client-server model a dedicated server holds the authoritative state and clients send requests that the server validates and applies. This pattern reduces cheating because clients cannot simply declare game events; the server enforces rules, corrects invalid movements, and broadcasts the official state. A peer-to-peer model instead has clients communicating directly and sharing state among themselves. That can be simpler for quick prototypes or small low-stakes games, but it makes preventing dishonest clients harder and increases the likelihood of divergent state if messages are lost or delayed. As a concrete example, imagine item collection: in client-server the client asks the server to pick up an item and the server checks if the item still exists and the pickup is legal. In peer-to-peer each client might accept the pickup locally and later resolve conflicts, which invites race conditions and exploits. A common misconception is that peer-to-peer is always cheaper: while it may reduce server costs, it raises complexity in reconciliation and security. Key takeaway: prefer client-server or host-client for competitive or persistent games where authoritative validation matters. Ask yourself: which parts of my game must be trusted and who should control them?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer
Core Concept

Two architecture patterns

Understand how messages flow and where validation happens.

Client-Server
  • Server holds authoritative state and validates clients.
  • Clients send actions via requests; server broadcasts updates.
  • Best for competitive or persistent games.
Peer-to-Peer
  • Clients share state directly without a central authority.
  • Simpler for small sessions but prone to cheating and divergence.
  • Requires reconciliation logic to resolve conflicts.
Example
Item collection validated by server to prevent false claims.
Common mistake
Allowing clients to authoritatively change critical game state without checks.
Quick comparison
Security
Client-server is stronger because server validates actions.
Complexity
Peer-to-peer may require complex conflict resolution code.
Key Takeaway

Choose client-server for authoritative control and fairness; use peer-to-peer only when small scope and simplicity outweigh security concerns.

screens.title: Netcode for GameObjects (NGO)
screens.narratorSegment: Netcode for GameObjects, or NGO, is Unity's officially supported framework for adding networking to GameObjects and their Components. It fits into the familiar GameObject model and provides primitives to mark objects for networked replication, to keep basic state synchronized, and to call remote methods. The central installation step is adding the package via the Package Manager. Once installed, the NetworkManager coordinates connections and spawning. A NetworkObject component marks any GameObject that should be visible and manageable across clients. Without a NetworkObject a GameObject remains local to the creating client. To synchronize simple values like health or position you use NetworkVariable. NetworkVariable replicates changes from server to clients automatically when the server updates the value. For one-shot or targeted communication, ServerRpc and ClientRpc let clients call server logic and the server call client logic respectively. A concrete example: mark a player prefab with a NetworkObject then add a NetworkVariable for health; when the server adjusts health, all clients receive the updated value without manual message plumbing. A common misconception is that NGO hides networking complexity entirely; it simplifies many tasks, but you still design authority, validation, and latency strategies. The key is using NGO primitives intentionally to enforce correctness and responsiveness.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Netcode for GameObjects
Definition

Netcode for GameObjects

Installable via Package Manager
Core primitives
  • NetworkObject — marks a GameObject for replication.
  • NetworkVariable<T> — replicates simple state from server to clients.
  • ServerRpc / ClientRpc — methods to call server or clients remotely.
Practical example
A player prefab with NetworkObject and a NetworkVariable for health ensures consistent health displays across all players when the server updates the value.
Pitfall
Assuming NetworkVariables replace all validation. They replicate values but you must decide who writes them.
Pro tip
Use ServerRpc for player inputs requiring validation, and ClientRpc for broadcast visuals.
Check
Verify initial NetworkVariable values are set on spawn and that clients receive updates.

screens.title: NetworkObject and NetworkVariable
screens.narratorSegment: NetworkObject and NetworkVariable are the basic building blocks for syncing GameObjects. A NetworkObject flags a GameObject to be spawned and managed across the network. Without it, instances remain local to the client that created them. NetworkVariables provide a typed way to keep primitive values consistent. When the server updates a NetworkVariable, NGO replicates that change to all connected clients automatically. Use NetworkVariable for values like health, score, or simplified position packets. For ownership patterns, a client can own a NetworkObject which allows local input to affect the object, but ownership does not remove the need for server validation. A concrete example from the provided starter code uses a NetworkVariable of type vector for position and an int for health; when the owner moves, it locally simulates movement and then requests the server to update the NetworkVariable. A common misconception is to treat NetworkVariable as instant and perfectly authoritative on clients; in practice there is latency and the server should be the source of truth for critical state. Key takeaway: mark what must be networked with NetworkObject, and use NetworkVariable to replicate simple state while designing clear write permissions.

keyIdea.text: NetworkObject marks networked GameObjects; NetworkVariable replicates typed state from server to clients automatically.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › NetworkObject & NetworkVariable
Process Flow

Mark and replicate

A simple lifecycle: spawn, update NetworkVariables, replicate to clients.

Spawn
Attach NetworkObject to prefabs so NetworkManager can spawn them across all peers.
Replicate
Update NetworkVariable on server; NGO sends changes to clients automatically.
Key Takeaway

Use NetworkObject to mark replicated prefabs and NetworkVariable for simple server-driven state replication.

Concrete example
Player prefab includes:
  • - NetworkObject component to spawn across clients
  • - NetworkVariable<Vector3> for position updates
  • - NetworkVariable<int> for health replicated from server
Misconception
NetworkVariables automatically secure state. In reality, write permissions and validation are design decisions you control.

screens.title: ServerRpc and ClientRpc
screens.narratorSegment: ServerRpc and ClientRpc are the mechanism for invoking logic across the network. A ServerRpc is called by a client and executed on the server. It is the usual path for client-originated actions that require validation, such as movement requests, firing weapons, or attempting to collect items. The server receives the request, checks game rules, updates authoritative state, and can change NetworkVariables or call ClientRpcs in response. A ClientRpc is called on the server and executed on clients; use it for broadcasting visual or audio feedback that every player should see. For instance, when the server applies damage it can call a ClientRpc to trigger a particle effect on all clients. An important concrete guideline is to avoid trusting client-sent data: treat ServerRpc calls as requests, not authoritative declarations. A common misconception is to use ClientRpc for critical state changes; ClientRpc is for notification and visual updates, not for authoritative writes. In practice, the flow looks like: client input -> ServerRpc -> server validation -> NetworkVariable update and/or ClientRpc broadcast. This clear flow preserves security while keeping clients responsive with local prediction where appropriate.

keyIdea.text: ServerRpc carries client requests to the server; ClientRpc broadcasts server-determined outcomes to clients.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › ServerRpc & ClientRpc
Process Flow

Request, validate, broadcast

Use ServerRpc for client requests and ClientRpc for server-driven notifications.

Typical flow
  1. Client sends ServerRpc with input intent.
  2. Server validates and updates authoritative state.
  3. Server updates NetworkVariables or calls a ClientRpc to notify clients.
Example
Client requests damage via ServerRpc; server subtracts health and calls a ClientRpc to play an effect everywhere.
Practical cards
Do
Use ServerRpc when clients need to request changes that require server validation.
Don't
Use ClientRpc to set critical authoritative state; it's intended for notifications and visuals.
Key Takeaway

Treat ServerRpc calls as requests to be validated, and use ClientRpc to reflect server-approved results back to players.

screens.title: Authority Models and Validation
screens.narratorSegment: Authority determines who can change a GameObject's state and who must validate those changes. In a server-authoritative model the server owns NetworkObjects and is the only entity that writes critical NetworkVariables. Clients send ServerRpc requests as intents, and the server decides and applies the changes. This model defends against cheating because clients cannot overwrite authoritative values. Client-authoritative models give clients more direct control, which can reduce server load and simplify input handling for single-player like features, but they are fragile in multiplayer because a malicious client could falsify state. Client ownership is sometimes used for local player movement where the owner predicts movement locally and sends updates to the server, but even then the server should validate collisions, resource collection, and combat. A concrete example from the chapter shows a player script where the owner moves locally and submits position updates to the server; the server can clamp or correct the position if it detects invalid movement. A common mistake is to assume ownership equals trust; always implement server checks for critical game rules. The learner question to reflect on is: which actions in your game absolutely require server validation and why?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Authority Models
Comparison

Server-authoritative vs Client-authoritative

Server-authoritative
Server writes critical state and validates client requests to prevent cheating and maintain consistency.
Client-authoritative
Clients can write state, useful for local responsiveness but requires trust and reconciliation when used in multiplayer.
Example and checks
In the example PlayerNetworkController the owner moves locally and sends position updates via a ServerRpc. The server can then validate and set the NetworkVariable for position if the movement is legal.
Common mistake
Assuming ownership implies trust. Always validate critical events on the server even for owned objects.
Key Takeaway

Designate server authority for rules that affect fairness; allow client ownership only for local responsiveness and always validate on server.

screens.title: PlayerNetworkController: Movement and Health
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the key networking behaviors in the PlayerNetworkController example. The script inherits from a network-aware base so it can access properties like IsOwner and IsHost. It declares NetworkVariables for position and health, which are the minimal replicated state for our demo. On spawn the script subscribes to health changes to update UI and optionally play effects. The Update loop differentiates the owner from remote players: the owner handles input and performs a local movement simulation for responsiveness, then uses a ServerRpc to request the server to update the NetworkVariable position. Non-owners simply set their transform from the replicated position value. When the owner fires a damage action we call a ServerRpc, which is executed on the server; the server reduces the Health NetworkVariable and optionally calls a ClientRpc to trigger a shared visual effect. Important design points are visible: owners perform local prediction, servers perform validation before changing NetworkVariables, and ClientRpc is used for visual feedback. A frequent misconception is saying ServerRpc equals trust; instead treat ServerRpc as a request and always validate. As an exercise, consider where you would add checks for teleporting or speed hacks in the server-side logic.

Synchronized Player Movement & Health

screens.title: Latency, Prediction, and Reconciliation
screens.narratorSegment: Network latency creates a tension between responsiveness and correctness. Clients expect instant feedback to input, but server validation introduces delay. A common pattern is client-side prediction: clients immediately simulate the results of their input locally so movement feels smooth, then send an authoritative request to the server. When the server replies with the official state, the client reconciles differences. For example, a client moves forward locally on key press and sends a ServerRpc with the new position. If the server detects that the client passed through a wall, it corrects the position and updates the NetworkVariable, which the client then applies, possibly with a visible correction. This reconciliation step must be carefully designed to avoid jarring snaps; smoothing or interpolation can help. Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Prediction & Reconciliation
Diagram

Prediction and reconciliation flow

Balance client responsiveness with server authority using prediction and reconciliation.

Client-side prediction
Client simulates movement immediately for responsiveness and queues the input for server validation.
Server validation
Server checks the requested state and updates authoritative NetworkVariables accordingly.
Reconciliation
Client applies server-provided state and smooths corrections to avoid abrupt visual snaps.
Concrete example
Owner moves locally and sends position updates. Server validates and corrects impossible movement; client reconciles to the server position.
Key Takeaway

Use prediction for responsiveness but always reconcile with server authority to avoid exploits and divergent state.

screens.title: Security, Disconnections, and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Robust multiplayer systems anticipate malicious clients, network failures, and bandwidth constraints. The foundational rule is to never trust the client with critical game logic. That means the server should calculate and distribute scores, apply damage resolution, and decide outcomes for contested resources. Implement server-side validation for positional sanity, resource pickups, and combat resolution. For disconnections, gracefully clean up server-side state and provide reconnect paths where appropriate; stale NetworkObjects or orphaned ownership can lead to inconsistent worlds. On performance, reduce bandwidth by sending only necessary updates, consider compressing data, and prefer NetworkVariables for frequent, small state changes. Logically group updates where possible to avoid unnecessary RPC bursts. A common developer mistake is putting heavy logic into ClientRpc calls or letting clients spam ServerRpcs without rate limiting. Also plan for error handling: handle RPC failures or partial updates, and ensure the game can recover from packet loss or reconnects. Key takeaway: secure authoritative logic on the server, handle disconnects clearly, and optimize data transfer to maintain responsiveness. Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Security & Performance

Security, Disconnections, and Performance

Practical strategies to keep your multiplayer game fair and stable.

Security
Always validate critical actions on the server and treat clients as untrusted.
Disconnects
Clean up orphaned objects, restore ownership or allow reconnection flows to maintain consistency.
Performance
Send only needed data, compress where possible, and use NetworkVariables for frequent small updates.
Common mistake
Allowing clients to directly modify authoritative values or relying on frequent unbatched RPCs.
Key Takeaway

Design with the assumption of malicious clients, plan reconnect behavior, and optimize data to preserve responsiveness and fairness.

screens.title: Testing and Assessment Ideas
screens.narratorSegment: Testing multiplayer features requires scenarios that reveal synchronization and authority issues. Start with the lab checks: run a host and a client and confirm movement and health updates match on both. Watch debug logs to ensure ServerRpc calls are received and processed on the server and that ClientRpc calls reach clients. Include stress tests where multiple clients perform simultaneous actions like item pickup to reveal race conditions. For assessment, ask targeted questions: which model prevents cheating for item collection and why; which Rpc type triggers particle effects on all clients. Use those exact questions to evaluate understanding. Also run negative tests: intentionally send invalid movement from a modified client and confirm the server corrects position. Performance tests should measure bandwidth used by frequent NetworkVariable updates, and you should try batching or reducing update rates where possible. A common oversight is not simulating packet loss or high latency during tests; include network throttling to observe client prediction and reconciliation behavior. Final takeaway: reproducible tests and scenario-based questions surface subtle bugs that casual testing misses. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential ideas you should carry forward. fullNarratorScript:
Multiplayer adds a new dimension to game development: you must keep many copies of the same world in agreement. In this chapter you will learn the essential architecture patterns used in Unity multiplayer, and practical tools in Netcode for GameObjects that make synchronization manageable. We begin by comparing client-server and peer-to-peer models and then take a hands-on path into Unity's Netcode primitives: NetworkObject, NetworkVariable, ServerRpc and ClientRpc. You'll also learn about authority—who can change state—and common defenses such as server validation and client-side prediction. The goal is not just to copy code, but to reason about trust, latency, and correctness when many players interact. For example, we'll use a simple player prefab with a NetworkObject and NetworkVariables for position and health to explore how changes propagate, how the server validates actions, and how to trigger visual effects safely. By the end, you will be able to set up a basic host-client test, explain why server authority prevents easy cheating, and identify where prediction or reconciliation is appropriate. Consider how your game would behave if a client lied about a score — that thought experiment will guide many design choices here.

In this chapter you'll build a working mental model of multiplayer design and the concrete skills to implement a basic synchronized demo in Unity. First, you'll be able to distinguish client-server and peer-to-peer architectures and explain when to choose each model. Next, you'll install and use Netcode for GameObjects to mark objects for networking and keep simple state synchronized. You will also learn how to design authority: when the server should be the final arbiter and when to allow a client limited ownership. Another objective is to synchronize player state using NetworkVariables and to trigger events with ServerRpc and ClientRpc calls. Each objective pairs a practical action with a rationale so you can justify a design choice for fairness, security, or responsiveness. For example, recognizing why server validation stops a cheating client will change how you structure item collection and scoring logic. These learning goals give you both the vocabulary and the actionable steps to build a small multiplayer prototype and evaluate its safety in real scenarios.

These objectives are deliberately practical: you will set up a NetworkManager, configure a Player Prefab with a NetworkObject, and confirm synchronization using a host and a client instance. You'll practice sending ServerRpc calls for input and ClientRpc calls for broadcast events, and you will observe how NetworkVariables replicate values like position and health. When testing, check that the authoritative server corrects invalid moves and that health updates originate on the server. For assessment, you should be able to answer why server authority prevents a client from arbitrarily increasing score and to pick the correct RPC type when you need a visual effect to run on every machine. You will also gain the habit of treating clients as untrusted, adding validation checks and handling disconnects gracefully. By the end, you will recognize common failure modes — such as stale state after a disconnect — and know where to add reconciliation or compression. These assessments map directly to the hands-on activity that follows.

Multiplayer architecture defines who holds the truth about the game world. In a client-server model a dedicated server holds the authoritative state and clients send requests that the server validates and applies. This pattern reduces cheating because clients cannot simply declare game events; the server enforces rules, corrects invalid movements, and broadcasts the official state. A peer-to-peer model instead has clients communicating directly and sharing state among themselves. That can be simpler for quick prototypes or small low-stakes games, but it makes preventing dishonest clients harder and increases the likelihood of divergent state if messages are lost or delayed. As a concrete example, imagine item collection: in client-server the client asks the server to pick up an item and the server checks if the item still exists and the pickup is legal. In peer-to-peer each client might accept the pickup locally and later resolve conflicts, which invites race conditions and exploits. A common misconception is that peer-to-peer is always cheaper: while it may reduce server costs, it raises complexity in reconciliation and security. Key takeaway: prefer client-server or host-client for competitive or persistent games where authoritative validation matters. Ask yourself: which parts of my game must be trusted and who should control them?

Netcode for GameObjects, or NGO, is Unity's officially supported framework for adding networking to GameObjects and their Components. It fits into the familiar GameObject model and provides primitives to mark objects for networked replication, to keep basic state synchronized, and to call remote methods. The central installation step is adding the package via the Package Manager. Once installed, the NetworkManager coordinates connections and spawning. A NetworkObject component marks any GameObject that should be visible and manageable across clients. Without a NetworkObject a GameObject remains local to the creating client. To synchronize simple values like health or position you use NetworkVariable. NetworkVariable replicates changes from server to clients automatically when the server updates the value. For one-shot or targeted communication, ServerRpc and ClientRpc let clients call server logic and the server call client logic respectively. A concrete example: mark a player prefab with a NetworkObject then add a NetworkVariable for health; when the server adjusts health, all clients receive the updated value without manual message plumbing. A common misconception is that NGO hides networking complexity entirely; it simplifies many tasks, but you still design authority, validation, and latency strategies. The key is using NGO primitives intentionally to enforce correctness and responsiveness.

NetworkObject and NetworkVariable are the basic building blocks for syncing GameObjects. A NetworkObject flags a GameObject to be spawned and managed across the network. Without it, instances remain local to the client that created them. NetworkVariables provide a typed way to keep primitive values consistent. When the server updates a NetworkVariable, NGO replicates that change to all connected clients automatically. Use NetworkVariable for values like health, score, or simplified position packets. For ownership patterns, a client can own a NetworkObject which allows local input to affect the object, but ownership does not remove the need for server validation. A concrete example from the provided starter code uses a NetworkVariable of type vector for position and an int for health; when the owner moves, it locally simulates movement and then requests the server to update the NetworkVariable. A common misconception is to treat NetworkVariable as instant and perfectly authoritative on clients; in practice there is latency and the server should be the source of truth for critical state. Key takeaway: mark what must be networked with NetworkObject, and use NetworkVariable to replicate simple state while designing clear write permissions.

ServerRpc and ClientRpc are the mechanism for invoking logic across the network. A ServerRpc is called by a client and executed on the server. It is the usual path for client-originated actions that require validation, such as movement requests, firing weapons, or attempting to collect items. The server receives the request, checks game rules, updates authoritative state, and can change NetworkVariables or call ClientRpcs in response. A ClientRpc is called on the server and executed on clients; use it for broadcasting visual or audio feedback that every player should see. For instance, when the server applies damage it can call a ClientRpc to trigger a particle effect on all clients. An important concrete guideline is to avoid trusting client-sent data: treat ServerRpc calls as requests, not authoritative declarations. A common misconception is to use ClientRpc for critical state changes; ClientRpc is for notification and visual updates, not for authoritative writes. In practice, the flow looks like: client input -> ServerRpc -> server validation -> NetworkVariable update and/or ClientRpc broadcast. This clear flow preserves security while keeping clients responsive with local prediction where appropriate.

Authority determines who can change a GameObject's state and who must validate those changes. In a server-authoritative model the server owns NetworkObjects and is the only entity that writes critical NetworkVariables. Clients send ServerRpc requests as intents, and the server decides and applies the changes. This model defends against cheating because clients cannot overwrite authoritative values. Client-authoritative models give clients more direct control, which can reduce server load and simplify input handling for single-player like features, but they are fragile in multiplayer because a malicious client could falsify state. Client ownership is sometimes used for local player movement where the owner predicts movement locally and sends updates to the server, but even then the server should validate collisions, resource collection, and combat. A concrete example from the chapter shows a player script where the owner moves locally and submits position updates to the server; the server can clamp or correct the position if it detects invalid movement. A common mistake is to assume ownership equals trust; always implement server checks for critical game rules. The learner question to reflect on is: which actions in your game absolutely require server validation and why?

Let's walk through the key networking behaviors in the PlayerNetworkController example. The script inherits from a network-aware base so it can access properties like IsOwner and IsHost. It declares NetworkVariables for position and health, which are the minimal replicated state for our demo. On spawn the script subscribes to health changes to update UI and optionally play effects. The Update loop differentiates the owner from remote players: the owner handles input and performs a local movement simulation for responsiveness, then uses a ServerRpc to request the server to update the NetworkVariable position. Non-owners simply set their transform from the replicated position value. When the owner fires a damage action we call a ServerRpc, which is executed on the server; the server reduces the Health NetworkVariable and optionally calls a ClientRpc to trigger a shared visual effect. Important design points are visible: owners perform local prediction, servers perform validation before changing NetworkVariables, and ClientRpc is used for visual feedback. A frequent misconception is saying ServerRpc equals trust; instead treat ServerRpc as a request and always validate. As an exercise, consider where you would add checks for teleporting or speed hacks in the server-side logic.

This lab walks you through creating a minimal synchronized player demo using Netcode for GameObjects.
